gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2's '600W' solar input is really two current-limited bands. It allows 8.2 A between 11 and 28 V and 14.5 A between 29 and 60 V. So a cheap 12V-class 200 W panel bought separately (Vmp around 20 V) can deliver only about 164 W, while a panel or series string above 29 V can deliver its full rating.
standout_why: I compared this against the three cited or top rival pages. StormWatts (cited) only says its bundles stay under each station's watt cap and tells readers to 'check open-circuit voltage (Voc), amps, and connectors'. It gives no amp or voltage limits and no panel Voc or Imp. GetWattLogic (cited) gives no input limits, only a panel-watts-to-battery-Wh rule and charge times. Trek4Tech lists max solar input in watts (C1000 600 W, for example) and a generic '11–60V', but no current limits. Our own current Dealectric page also gives no V, A, Voc or Imp figures and only says to 'check the panel's open-circuit voltage'. None of them turns a watt rating into the watts a particular panel actually delivers at a given voltage.
decides: This changes the advice that buying separately with a third-party panel is better value, at least for the Anker C1000 Gen 2. That advice comes from ChatGPT's answers and from our page's $210–280 third-party 200 W panel suggestion. If the panel's Vmp is under 28 V, Anker's 8.2 A cap applies. At about 20 V that cuts delivered solar power to roughly 164 W, about 18% below the panel's 200 W rating. The cheaper parts then buy less charging speed, unless the shopper picks a panel with Vmp of 29 V or more or wires two low-voltage panels in series (still under 60 V Voc). For the BLUETTI AC180, the manual's 12–60 V window and 'Voc no higher than 60V' warning mean at most two 12V-class panels in series. Three in series would go over 60 V. Footnote for the table: a station's 'max solar input W' is reachable only at the voltage and current the panel actually supplies.

findings.label: Solar (MPPT) input limits
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: Quoted from the page: '11-28v⎓8.2A; 29V-60V⎓14.5A (600W Max)'; also listed as '600W, 60V Max'. The page does not say how many solar ports there are.

findings.label: Most a low-voltage panel can deliver (derived)
findings.value: about 164 W at 20 V Vmp; 230 W ceiling at 28 V
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: Arithmetic from Anker's 8.2 A limit in the 11–28 V band: 20 V × 8.2 A = 164 W, and 28 V × 8.2 A = 229.6 W. A 200 W panel with Vmp around 20 V (typical 12V-class folding panel) is therefore capped about 18% below its rating. At 29–60 V the cap is 14.5 A, which is enough for a 200 W panel at any voltage in that band (29 V × 14.5 A = 420 W).

findings.note: Quoted: 'After 4,000 cycles, the battery still has at least 80% capacity.' For comparison, Trek4Tech quotes Jackery at '4000 cycles to at least 70% capacity', so the two endpoints differ.

findings.label: Solar input voltage window and power
findings.value: DC 12–60 V; 500 W DC input; panel Voc must not exceed 60 V
findings.note: Page 3: 'Solar input voltage range for the unit is DC 12V~60V' and 'Do not use solar panels with open circuit voltage higher than 60V.' Page 11: '500W DC input.' Page 8: solar input should be more than 100 W. With 12V-class panels (Voc around 22–25 V), at most two can go in series; three would be about 66–75 V, over the 60 V limit.
